https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
An election timetable prepared for the Troy School District 2022 Capital Improvement Bond Proposal, oriented to a November 8, 2022 election date, with the bonds to be qualified under the Michigan School Bond Qualification and Loan Program. The document lays out the sequence of required actions and deadlines to place the bond proposal before the electorate.

The timetable's milestones are as follows. May 17, 2022 -- Board action: a Board resolution to approve the proposed bond projects and the not-to-exceed amount of bonds, and to authorize preparation of the Application for Preliminary Qualification required for participation in the Michigan School Bond Qualification and Loan Program. May/June 2022 -- Prepare Application for Preliminary Qualification: with the assistance of the architect, construction manager, owner's representative, bond counsel, and financial advisor, the district will complete a draft of the Application, which will include the bond projects; the size of the bond issue and number of series; a utilization and capacity analysis; debt millage schedules; construction drawdown and investment earnings; an enrollment projection; and ballot language.

June 15, 2022 -- Treasury meeting: a preliminary meeting with the Department of Treasury, held via conference call at 10:00 a.m. (Microsoft Teams); the Application for Preliminary Qualification must be submitted to the Department of Treasury at least three working days prior to this meeting. June 21, 2022 -- Board action: a Board resolution to approve submission of the Application for Preliminary Qualification to the Department of Treasury. July 25, 2022 -- Treasury approval: approval from the Department of Treasury on the Application for Preliminary Qualification, allowing 30 days from submission.

July 26, 2022 -- Board action: a Board resolution certifying the bond proposal to its Election Coordinator (the Oakland County Clerk) for submission to the electors at the bond election date. On or before August 16, 2022 -- Submission of bond proposal: the district must submit the certified bond proposal to its Election Coordinator (the Oakland County Clerk) no later than 4 p.m. on this date, which is the twelfth Tuesday before the bond election date. Tuesday, November 8, 2022 -- Bond election date.

It lays out the potential bond program scope building by building rather than by dollar figure, grouping proposed work under columns for Athens High School; TCCHS, IAE and TCT; "Other Items"; Troy High School; Smith Middle School; Baker Middle School; Boulan Park / Larson Middle Schools; and Troy Preschool & Elementary Schools.

For Troy High School, the document lists upgrades to address circulation issues, student collaboration enhancements, multi-use space for robotics, fitness and other activities, and other critical program needs, plus expanding music rehearsal spaces and adding new rehearsal space, and athletic upgrades. The IAE scope calls for a new academic wing and major renovation of remaining academic spaces, together with fine and performing arts upgrades and athletic upgrades.

The Oakland Schools Board of Education "2022 Election Timeline," a reference calendar issued to constituent districts (including the Troy School District) governing the biennial election of intermediate school district board members, in which each constituent district casts a vote through a designated representative.

The timeline begins on December 6, 2021, when candidates could pick up nominating petitions and affidavit forms at the Oakland County Clerk's Office, Elections Division, located at 1200 N. Telegraph Road, Dept. 417, Pontiac, MI 48341. The deadline for candidates to file nominating petitions, filing fees, and affidavits of identity with the County Clerk's Elections Division was 4:00 PM on May 6, 2022. On May 9, 2022, Oakland Schools receives the official candidate list from the County Clerk and forwards it to constituent district superintendents and their executive assistants.

By May 16, 2022, each constituent district board of education must (1) designate its representative and identify the ISD candidate(s) its board supports, and (2) consider and adopt a resolution affirming those choices - with each board required to consider its resolution at not less than one public meeting before adoption. Copies of the district resolutions were due to the Oakland Schools administrative office by 4:00 PM on June 3, 2022, via fax (248.209.2206) or email (Nicole.Christian@oakland.k12.mi.us); the notice stresses that no approved resolutions would be accepted after that date and that a district failing to file would be unable to cast a vote at the June 6 election.

On June 6, 2022, from 5:30 to 7:30 PM, district representatives attend the Oakland Schools Board of Education Biennial Board Election open meeting to cast ballots on behalf of their districts, with no absentee ballots accepted. Notification of election results is sent on June 7, 2022 to constituent superintendents, their executive assistants, and the County Clerk's Elections Division. Finally, on July 11, 2022, successful candidates take the Oath of Office at the Oakland Schools Board of Education Organizational Meeting if they were not present at the Biennial Board Election.

It provides that intermediate school board members are elected biennially on the first Monday in June by an electoral body of one representative designated by each constituent district's board via resolution, that members serve six-year terms beginning July 1, and that candidates are nominated by petition or a $100 filing fee, with no more than two members from the same district.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A reprint of THE REVISED SCHOOL CODE (EXCERPT), Act 451 of 1976, Section 380.614, courtesy of the Michigan Legislature, rendered February 17, 2022 - the statute governing election of intermediate school board members.

Key provisions
- Members are elected biennially on the first Monday in June by an electoral body of one person designated by each constituent district board.
- Each constituent board designates its representative by resolution adopted not earlier than 21 days before the election, considered at 1 or more public meetings and passed by majority vote; the resolution must identify the candidate(s) the board supports and direct its representative to vote for them at least on the first ballot.
- The ISD secretary must mail certified notice of the meeting to each constituent district secretary at least 10 days ahead; the meeting is an open meeting under the Open Meetings Act (1976 PA 267).
- Terms are 6 years, beginning July 1; no more than 2 members from the same district (unless districts are fewer than seats).
- Vacancies are filled by remaining members until the next biennial election; the state board fills a vacancy not filled within 30 days.
- Nominating petitions require 40-100 signatures where ISD population is 10,000 or more (6-20 if under 10,000); alternatively a candidate may pay a nonrefundable $100 filing fee.

Purpose
Provide the statutory authority underlying the Oakland Schools biennial ISD board election in which Troy participates.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A verbatim excerpt of Michigan's Revised School Code, Act 451 of 1976, Section 614 (MCL 380.614), reproduced courtesy of the Michigan Legislature and rendered current through Public Act 8 of 2022. It sets out the procedures for electing members of an intermediate school board and was supplied as legal background for the Oakland Schools intermediate district board election.

Subsection (1) provides that, except as provided in section 615 and subject to MCL 168.642c, intermediate school board members are elected biennially on the first Monday in June by an electoral body composed of one person designated by the board of each constituent school district. Subsection (2) requires each constituent district board to designate its representative by resolution adopted not earlier than 21 days before the biennial election, considered at not less than one public meeting before adoption and passed by a majority vote of the members serving; the resolution must identify the candidate the board supports for each position to be filled and direct its representative to vote for that individual at least on the first ballot. The secretary of the intermediate school board must send certified-mail notice of the hour and place of the meeting to each constituent district's board secretary at least 10 days beforehand; the intermediate board's president and secretary act as chairperson and secretary, and the meeting is an open meeting conducted under the Open Meetings Act, 1976 PA 267, MCL 15.261 to 15.275.

Subsection (3) fixes the term of office at six years, beginning July 1 following election, and provides that not more than two members of the intermediate board may be from the same school district unless there are fewer districts than positions to fill. Subsection (4) addresses vacancies: they are filled by the remaining members until the next biennial election (when the balance of the unexpired term is filled), notice must be filed with the state board within five days, and if a vacancy is not filled within 30 days the state board fills it.

Subsections (5) through (7) govern nominations: a candidate must be nominated by petitions signed by school electors of the combined constituent districts - a minimum of 6 and maximum of 20 signatures if the ISD population is under 10,000, or a minimum of 40 and maximum of 100 if it is 10,000 or more - with petitions and an affidavit under MCL 168.558 filed with the school district filing official not later than 30 days before the election. Alternatively, a candidate may pay a nonrefundable $100.00 filing fee, which has the same effect as filing petitions. The excerpt closes with the statute's amendment history from 1977 through 2011.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A Business Office memorandum from Rick West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, to Superintendent Dr. Rich Machesky, dated June 10, 2022, regarding the Troy School District's proposed 2022-2023 millage rates. Taxable valuation amounts were received from the Oakland County Equalization Department; overall, the District's taxable valuation on all property increased by $298,030,680, or 6.88%, from the previous year, with increases in both homestead and non-homestead property. West notes that taxable valuations drive the district's hold-harmless, local non-homestead, sinking fund, and debt retirement revenue. The L-4029 tax-levy form is attached.

Hold-Harmless Millage Rate: levied so the district receives its full per-pupil foundation allowance, it is authorized to generate $786 per student, which is $248.18 less than the $1,034.18 per student authorized before the re-establishment of 20j/m, a change that shifted the revenue obligation from local taxpayers to the state. Levied only on homestead property, the proposed 2022-23 hold-harmless rate is 3.0693 mills, a decrease of 0.3185 mills from the current 3.3878, attributed to rising taxable values and lower assumed student enrollment.

Non-Homestead Millage Rate: all Michigan districts may levy up to 18.0000 mills, with voter approval, on non-homestead property (chiefly commercial and industrial real property; homeowners do not pay it on a principal residence). The proposed 2022-23 non-homestead rate is 18.00 mills.

Commercial Personal Property Millage Rate: since 2008-09, commercial personal property is treated as homestead for Headlee rollback purposes and exempt from the first 12 mills of non-homestead operating millage, reduced by the hold-harmless millage. The resulting rate is 9.0693 mills (18 - 12 + 3.0693), down from 9.3878 mills in 2021-22.

Industrial Personal Property Millage Rate: since 2008-09, industrial personal property is classified as homestead and exempt from the entire 18 mills of non-homestead operating millage, reduced by the hold-harmless millage; the resulting rate is 3.0693 mills, identical to the homeowner hold-harmless rate and down from 3.3878 mills in 2021-22.

Debt Retirement Millage Rate: the Debt Retirement Fund pays principal and interest on general long-term debt, funded primarily by a debt-retirement property-tax levy. The proposed 2022-23 rate is 4.1000 mills, unchanged from the current year's 4.1000 mills; combined with the debt retirement fund balance, it is expected to be sufficient to meet the district's 2022-23 debt obligations.

Sinking Fund Millage Rate: the Sinking Fund, approved by the community in November 2017 for building and site infrastructure improvements and repairs, is funded by a building-and-site sinking-fund levy. The proposed 2022-23 rate is 0.9651 mills, a 0.0129-mill decrease from the current 0.9780 mills, due to the millage reduction factor required by the Headlee amendment (which caps taxable-value growth at the rate of inflation). Estimated sinking-fund revenue for 2022-23 is $4,442,000.

Millage certification by the Board of Education is scheduled to occur at the June 21, 2022 Board of Education meeting. The memo issued from the Business Office at 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098.

A Board of Education presentation from June 2022 introducing the Troy School District's 2026 Blueprint (Project 2026) and its accountability plan. The presentation refreshes the district's mission and vision, stating a mission of 'Ensuring learning for all' that centers the ONETROY community, and organizes work around four themes: Early Childhood to Career, Equity and Well-Being, Deep Learning, and Building Capacity. The 'World Class for All' pillars are aligned to core values of Collaboration, Deep Learning, and Focus, and the accountability plan holds the team to Objectives and Key Results.

Green Pillar (Early Childhood to Career): Objectives include continuing to invest in high-quality early childhood education and advocating for universal preschool access for all three- and four-year-olds, and expanding college and career pathways for middle and high school students through high-quality career and technical education (CTE), computer science access, connections for underrepresented students to in-demand careers, and work-based learning with higher-education and employer partners that let students earn credentials or college credit. Key results for 2021-22 include applying for 16-32 additional GSRP slots from the state of Michigan, opening 2-3 additional PreK classrooms (40-60 students), scheduling two meetings or site visits with local legislators regarding free preschool for all, having building leaders participate twice in Career Readiness meetings, and researching and developing a Portrait of a Graduate framework and survey by the close of the school year. January-June 2022 celebrations note that early childhood enrollment is at a record high with waitlists for PreK, GSRP, tuition, and before-and-after-school programs; that the Portrait of a Graduate team has created a timeline; and that CTE program growth provided almost triple the funding from 2020-21 to 2021-22. Challenges include capacity limits for early childhood programs and that the grantee, Oakland Schools, has not offered access to additional GSRP slots, plus alignment of Media/Maker spaces with Career Readiness. Recommendations include early and frequent early childhood recruitment for 2022-23, aligning PreK enrollment with kindergarten enrollment, continued advocacy for universal funding, and messaging Career Readiness as a tool aligned with academic and college planning.

Red Pillar (Equity and Well-Being): Objectives include safely reopening schools and supporting students disproportionately impacted by the pandemic; funding investments to support the whole child, including community schools with wraparound services such as afterschool programs and hiring more counselors, social workers, and school psychologists; and assessing the need for upgraded facilities to meet the demands of a world-class learning environment. Key results include increasing social work and counseling support in all buildings, targeting 1.0 social worker at every elementary school with increased psychologist support and counseling at the secondary level, reviewing and monitoring student data, emphasizing adult learning in well-being and equity, creating a common understanding of a system of support, and developing a district-level Equity Leader network. The presentation was delivered at the June 14, 2022 Board of Education Workshop.

The form must be completed and submitted on or before September 30, 2022, with the original going to the county clerk(s) and the Michigan Department of Treasury and copies to the equalization department(s) and each township or city clerk. It is issued under the authority of MCL Sections 211.24e, 211.34, and 211.34d; filing is mandatory and a penalty applies for non-filing under MCL Section 211.119. The form records the county or counties where the local government unit levies taxes and the 2022 taxable value of all properties in the unit as of 5-23-2022, and for local school districts the 2022 taxable value excluding principal residence, qualified agricultural, qualified forest, and industrial and commercial personal properties. Its columns capture, for each millage: the source (column 1); purpose of millage such as operating, debt service, school enhancement, or sinking fund (column 2); date of election (column 3); original millage authorized by election, charter, etc. (column 4); the 2021 millage rate permanently reduced by MCL 211.34d 'Headlee' rollback (column 5); the 2022 current-year Headlee millage reduction fraction (column 6); the 2022 permanently reduced rate (column 7); the Sec. 211.34 truth in assessing or equalization millage rollback fraction (column 8); the maximum allowable millage levy (column 9); millage requested to be levied July 1 and December 1 (columns 10 and 11); and the expiration date of the authorized millage (column 12). The certification language affirms that the requested levy rates have been reduced as necessary to comply with the state constitution (Article 9, Section 31) and with MCL Sections 211.24e, 211.34, and, for local school districts levying a Supplemental (Hold Harmless) Millage, 380.1211(3), and provides for signatures by the clerk/secretary and chairperson/president. The instructions note that a local school district must separately list operating millages as 'Operating ALL' (levied on all properties, such as Supplemental Hold Harmless and Building and Site Sinking Fund millages) versus 'Operating NON-HOME' (levied on all properties excluding principal residence, qualified agricultural, qualified forest, and industrial personal properties, such as the 18 mills in a district that does not levy a Supplemental Hold Harmless millage), and reference State Tax Commission Bulletin 2 of 2022. Preamble (WHEREAS clauses). The resolution opens by stating that the safety and well-being of students, teachers, and staff is a top priority in the Troy School District. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose: The official ballot language for a School Improvement Bond Proposition to be presented to voters of the Troy School District, County of Oakland, State of Michigan. The proposition asks whether the district shall borrow a sum not to exceed Five Hundred Fifty-Five Million Dollars ($555,000,000) and issue its general obligation unlimited tax bonds, in one or more series, to pay for four categories of projects: (1) remodeling, equipping, re-equipping, furnishing and re-furnishing school buildings, athletic fields, playgrounds and other facilities to create a modern learning environment for students and for health, safety, security and other purposes; (2) erecting, completing, equipping and furnishing a replacement middle school and classroom additions and other additions to existing school buildings and other facilities; (3) acquiring and installing instructional technology infrastructure and equipment in school buildings and other facilities; and (4) acquiring sites, preparing, developing and improving sites at school buildings and other facilities and the purchase of school buses. Voters mark YES or NO. The ballot states that the annual debt millage required to retire all bonds of the district currently outstanding and proposed is expected to be at or below 6.10 mills, which is a 2 mill increase from the 4.10 mills of annual debt millage levied in 2022. The maximum number of years any series of bonds may be outstanding, exclusive of refunding, is not more than thirty (30) years; the estimated millage to be levied in the first year is 3.35 mills (equal to $3.35 per $1,000 of taxable value); and the estimated simple average annual millage required to retire each series is 3.94 mills ($3.94 per $1,000 of taxable value). If approved by the voters, the bonds will be guaranteed by the State under the School Bond Qualification and Loan Program; the district currently has $116,165,000 of qualified bonds outstanding and $0 of qualified loans outstanding under the Program, and does not expect to borrow from the Program to pay debt service on these bonds. The ballot notes that the estimated computed millage rate may change in the future based on changed circumstances, and that, pursuant to State law, expenditure of bond proceeds must be audited and the proceeds cannot be used for teacher, administrator or employee salaries, repair or maintenance costs or other operating expenses.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A memorandum dated July 19, 2022, on Troy School District Business Office letterhead (4400 Livernois; phone 248.823.4022, fax 248.823.4013), addressed from Rick West, Assistant Superintendent of Business Services, to Superintendent Dr. Rich Machesky, regarding the 2022-23 food service lunch price adjustment.

The memo explains that the National School Lunch Program (NSLP) requires school food authorities (SFAs) to ensure sufficient funds are provided to the nonprofit school food service account for lunches served to students not certified eligible for free or reduced-price meals; in other words, free and reduced-price reimbursements may not subsidize the district's paid lunches. The USDA Food and Nutrition Service paid lunch equity (PLE) tool was created to help SFAs calculate their required paid lunch price increase under Section 205 of the Healthy, Hunger-Free Kids Act of 2010. The calculation multiplies the number of paid meals served in October of the prior fiscal year by the price per meal to determine a weighted-average paid price, which must meet or exceed the difference between the NSLP free-meal and paid-meal reimbursement rates; if it does not, an adjustment is required.

The tool's result requires Troy School District to raise paid lunch prices. The prior calculation yielded a weighted average of $2.54, while the requirement for 2022-23 is $3.30. West recommends a $0.60 increase per elementary paid lunch and a $0.60 average increase for variable-priced secondary paid lunches, producing a new weighted-average price of $3.49. This exceeds the $3.30 requirement and is expected to sustain the district for a few years. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
An instructional excerpt from the USDA Food and Nutrition Service (FNS) Paid Lunch Equity (PLE) Tool for School Year (SY) 2022-23, provided as an attachment to the Troy School District food service lunch price adjustment considered on July 26, 2022. The text is generic federal guidance for the contiguous states rather than district-specific figures.

It explains that for SY 2022-23, SFAs that, on a weighted average, charged less than the target weighted-average price of $3.31 for paid lunches in SY 2021-22 are required to adjust their weighted-average lunch price or add non-Federal funds to the nonprofit school food service account. Higher targets apply outside the contiguous states: $3.87 in Hawaii, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico, and $5.37 in Alaska. SFAs must use their unrounded adjusted average paid lunch price requirement from SY 2021-22 when calculating the SY 2022-23 increase; if an SFA rounded down (for example, a $2.98 unrounded requirement rounded to $2.95), the next year's calculation is still based on the unrounded figure.

The guidance addresses credits and shortfalls: if an SFA raised its weighted-average paid lunch price above the required amount in SY 2021-22, the excess may be subtracted from the SY 2022-23 requirement, and SFAs must keep records to carry forward the calculations; if the SFA did not raise prices enough, the shortfall carries forward.

For SFAs choosing to contribute non-Federal sources in lieu of raising prices, the required contribution is determined by multiplying the total number of paid reimbursable lunches claimed for the prior year by the difference between the SY 2021-22 weighted-average price requirement and the actual SY 2021-22 weighted-average price. Beginning in SY 2013-14, FNS expanded the definition of a non-Federal source; eligible sources include per-meal non-Federal reimbursement for any paid meal (breakfast, lunch, etc.), any funds provided by organizations for any paid meal, and any proportion attributable to paid meals from direct payments made from school district funds to support lunch service.

The excerpt also describes the SY 2022-23 PLE Tool itself: its first tab contains detailed instructions, and the tool calculates the weighted-average paid lunch price for SY 2021-22, the required average weighted increase for SY 2022-23, and any required non-Federal source contribution, accounting for prior-year credits and shortfalls. A split feature lets SFAs meet the requirement partly by raising prices and partly by contributing non-Federal funds. To use it, SFAs need their SY 2021-22 unrounded price requirement (or the SY 2010-11 weighted-average price), all paid lunch prices for October 2021, and the number of paid lunches served at each price in October 2021.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose: The Michigan High School Athletic Association (MHSAA) Athletes and Officials Accident Medical and Concussion Insurance summary outlines coverage the MHSAA has provided since the 1970-71 school year to participants at each member school and to all registered officials, intended to help pay excess accident medical bills for injuries sustained in athletic activities under MHSAA jurisdiction. Coverage applies to grades 6-12 students accidentally injured while engaged in interscholastic athletic activities in sports that end with an MHSAA tournament, including baseball, boys and girls basketball, boys and girls bowling, boys and girls cross country, football, boys and girls golf, girls gymnastics, girls competitive cheer, ice hockey, boys and girls lacrosse, boys and girls soccer, girls softball, boys and girls alpine skiing, boys and girls swimming and diving, boys and girls tennis, boys and girls track and field, girls volleyball, and wrestling. Eligible athletes are covered while participating in season under the direct supervision of a full-time school employee or designated coach and while traveling directly to and from scheduled events in school-sponsored transportation. Students ineligible under MHSAA regulations are not covered, though students ineligible only under local school rules, or suspended from contests under Regulation V, Section 3, remain covered if allowed to keep practicing with the team. The coverage is provided at no cost to eligible athletes and officials; the MHSAA is the policyholder and pays the premium. The policy pays up to $1,000,000 in medical expenses after a $25,000 paid-medical-expense deductible per claim, covering expenses left unpaid by the parents' or official's insurance or other sources such as school-purchased insurance. A cash benefit of up to $50,000 is payable if a covered person is paralyzed or in a coma within 180 days after the accident, made after a physician certifies, following a 16-month waiting period, that the injury is permanent and irreversible. The first medical expense must be incurred within 90 days of the accident, and a $10,000 accidental death or dismemberment benefit is paid if either event occurs within 365 days. Sideline cheerleaders are covered while traveling to and from and while cheering at interscholastic events under school-employee supervision, provided their activity does not exceed MHSAA Girls Competitive Cheer safety norms for the height of mounts, flips, and stunts. The coverage excludes any out-of-season activities and activities beyond the mileage limits of Regulation II, Section 6, Interpretation 193. Separately, Concussion Care Insurance, provided since the 2015-16 school year to MHSAA member junior high/middle schools and high schools, pays accident medical expense benefits for a suspected concussion sustained during an in-season covered activity (practice or competition), with a policy limit of $25,000 per accident. The claims administrator is Bryan Cronen of First Agency, Inc., 5071 West H Avenue, Kalamazoo, MI 49009-8501 (phone 269.381.6630, fax 269.381.3055). The document instructs districts to ensure all high schools and junior high/middle schools are designated by the Board of Education as MHSAA member schools so athletes at both levels are covered by the MHSAA-purchased plan.

Under High School Regulations: Regulation I, Section 1(F) revised cooperative-program rules so that two or more member high schools with combined enrollment not exceeding 3,500 students may, with Executive Committee approval, conduct a cooperative program in specified sports sponsored by 250 or fewer schools -- girls gymnastics, boys and girls lacrosse, boys and girls alpine skiing, and boys and girls swimming and diving -- while ice hockey cooperatives are allowed up to a combined 5,500 enrollment; the enrollment maximums may be waived for up to four years under stated participation conditions, and a cooperative program may not exist beyond four school years. Regulation I, Section 7 reinstated the previous academic credit record regulation that had been suspended since May 2020 due to the pandemic. Regulation I, Section 9, Interpretation 65 (Transfers) clarified that references to "parent/parents" include stepparents and defined the "family unit" to always include parents and minor siblings, potentially extending to adult siblings, stepsiblings, aunts, uncles, grandparents, and significant others who have lived in the dwelling at least 12 months. Regulation I, Section 11 (Amateur Status/Awards) barred a student from being paid or given merchandise or privileges in exchange for a commercial endorsement, autograph, photograph, or appearance fee based on athletic participation, ability, achievements, or potential in MHSAA tournament sports, and prohibited posing in the school's athletic uniform to promote a for-profit or non-profit non-school commercial enterprise even if unpaid. Regulation II, Section 6 added Minnesota to border-state references for contests with out-of-state schools. Regulation II, Section 11(H) and Interpretation 233 addressed school transportation, prohibiting its use for out-of-season school-year activities while permitting summer use with school-district approval funded by booster clubs, teams, student groups, or community, civic, or service groups rather than general school operating funds; "school transportation" includes vehicles owned or leased by the district or operated by any entity the district contracts with. Regulation II, Section 14(B), approved in December and effective immediately, revised video-streaming rules to allow schools to distribute live regular-season video. The document notes it does not include all Council action.
